After this she asks, "And how fares the king?" He says, "He has fled." And she rejoins, "For this Tissaphernes is to blame to him." And again she asks, "And where is Cyrus now?" The messenger answers, "Where good men ought to bivouac." Going on little by little and step by step, barely at last, as the saying is, he broke it out — most expressively in character and vividly, both showing the messenger reporting the calamity unwillingly, and throwing the mother into anxiety, and the hearer too.

Vividness also arises from telling the concomitants of things, as someone said of the boor walking, that "the noise of his feet was heard from afar as he approached, as though he were not walking, but as it were kicking the earth."

And what Plato says of Hippocrates, "blushing — for day had already begun to show somewhat — so that he became visible," that this is most vivid is plain to everyone; and the vividness has arisen from the care about the account and from recalling that Hippocrates had come to him by night.
Cacophony too is often vivid, as in "He smote, and out the brain," and "and many an up-slope, down-slope"; for by the cacophony it has imitated the unevenness; and all imitation has something vivid.

Coined words too produce vividness, through being brought out in imitation, as "lapping." But if he had said "drinking," he would neither have imitated the dogs drinking, nor would any vividness have arisen. And the "with their tongues" added to "lapping" makes the passage yet more vivid. So much about vividness, to speak summarily.

Persuasiveness lies in two things, in the clear and in the ordinary; for the unclear and the unusual is unpersuasive. So one must pursue, in persuasiveness, an expression that is neither elaborate nor overblown, and likewise a composition that is steady and has nothing rhythm-like.

Persuasiveness lies in these, then, and in what Theophrastus says, that one ought not to discourse at full length and with precision about everything, but to leave some things for the hearer too to understand and reckon out for himself. For when he has understood what was left out by you, he becomes not merely your hearer but your witness, and at the same time more well-disposed. For he thinks himself intelligent through you, who gave him the occasion to understand; whereas to tell everything as to a fool is like passing judgment that the hearer is witless.

Since the epistolary style too requires plainness, we shall speak about it as well. Artemon, who edited the letters of Aristotle, says that one ought to write a dialogue and letters in the same manner, for the letter is, as it were, one half of the dialogue.

And he says something, perhaps, but not the whole. For the letter ought to be somewhat more carefully wrought than the dialogue; for the dialogue imitates a man speaking offhand, whereas the letter is written and sent as a gift, in a way.

Who, then, would converse with a friend as Aristotle does, writing to Antipater on behalf of the exiled old man, when he says, "But if this man is gone, an exile to all the ends of the earth, so as not to be brought back, it is plain that no one grudges those who wish to go down to Hades"? For one who converses thus resembles a man making a display rather than talking.

Frequent disjunctions, too, do not befit letters; for disjunction is unclear in writing, and the imitative quality is not so proper to writing as to debate, as in the Euthydemus: "Who was it, Socrates, with whom you were conversing yesterday in the Lyceum? Surely a great crowd stood round you." And a little further on he adds, "But he seems to me to be some stranger, the man you were conversing with; who was it?" For all such expression and imitation would befit an actor rather than written letters.

Let the letter have a great deal of the ethical character, like the dialogue; for nearly everyone writes a kind of image of his own soul in the letter. From every other kind of discourse too one can see the character of the writer, but from none so well as from a letter.

Let the size of the letter be kept within bounds, as also the expression. Those that are too long, and moreover too bulky in their expression, would not in truth be letters, but treatises with "Greetings" written at the head — like many of Plato's, and that of Thucydides.

And let it be rather loosely constructed; for it is absurd to build periods, as though one were writing not a letter but a forensic speech. And it is not merely absurd, but not even friendly, to practice such things in letters, when, as the proverb says, one should be "calling figs figs."

One must know that not only the expression but also certain subjects are epistolary. Aristotle, at any rate, who seems above all to have succeeded in the epistolary, says, "This I do not write to you, for it was not epistolary."

For if anyone should write sophistries and natural philosophy in a letter, he writes indeed, but he does not write a letter. For the letter aims to be a kind of brief friendly greeting, and the setting-out of a simple matter in simple words.

Its beauty lies in friendly courtesies and in the close-set proverbs in it; and let this alone of cleverness be in it, since the proverb is something popular and common, whereas the man who utters maxims and exhorts seems no longer to be talking through a letter, but from a stage-machine.

Aristotle, however, sometimes uses even proofs in an epistolary way, as when, wishing to teach that one ought to do good to great cities and small alike, he says, "For the gods are equal in both; so that, since the Graces are goddesses, equal ones will be laid up for you with both." For both what he proves is epistolary, and the proof itself.

Since we sometimes write to cities and to kings, let such letters be a little elevated. For one must take into account the person to whom one writes; elevated, however, not so as to be a treatise instead of a letter, like the letters of Aristotle to Alexander, and Plato's to the kinsfolk of Dion.
In general let the letter be mixed, in respect of expression, out of these two styles, the graceful and the plain. So much about the letter, and at the same time about the plain style.

Beside the plain too lies a faulty style, the so-called dry. This too arises in three things. In the thought, as someone said of Xerxes, that "Xerxes came down with all his own folk." For he greatly diminished the matter, saying "with all his own folk" instead of "with all Asia."

The dry arises in the expression when one reports a great matter in small words, as the Gadarene does of the sea-fight at Salamis; and of Phalaris the tyrant someone said, "For Phalaris was annoying the Acragantines somewhat." For so great a sea-fight, and the savagery of tyrants, one ought not to express by the word "somewhat" nor by "annoying," but in great words befitting the underlying matter.

The dry arises in composition either when the phrases are dense, as in the Aphorisms: "Life is short, but art is long, the moment is fleeting, experience treacherous"; or when, in a great matter, the clause is cut short and not full, as when someone, accusing Aristides because he did not come to the sea-fight at Salamis but came uninvited, said that "Demeter came and fought at sea too, but Aristides did not." For the cutting-off is both unfitting and untimely. Such cuttings-off must be used in other contexts.

Often, indeed, the thought itself is frigid and, as we now call it, affected, but the composition is cut short and steals away the offensiveness of the thought, as in the case of the man who lay with a dead woman, when someone said that "he does not, in turn, lie with the woman." For the thought is plain even to a blind man, they say, but the composition, contracted, somehow steals the offence of the matter, and produces what now has the name "dry affectation," compounded of two faults: of affectation through the matter, and of dryness through the composition.

And the points about forcefulness would now be clear from what has been said before, that it too would arise in the three things in which the previous styles arise. For some subjects are of themselves forceful, so that those who speak of them seem forceful, even if they do not speak forcefully, as Theopompus, speaking of the flute-girls in the Piraeus and the brothels and the flute-players and singers and dancers — all these being forceful words, even though he spoke weakly, seems forceful.

In respect of composition, this style would arise first if it should have phrases instead of clauses; for length dissolves vehemence, whereas much shown in little is more forceful. An example is the "Of the Lacedaemonians to Philip, Dionysius in Corinth"; but if they had drawn it out, "Dionysius, fallen from his rule, lives as a beggar in Corinth teaching letters," it would have been a narrative almost rather than an abuse.
In other matters too the Spartans were by nature brief in speech; for the brief and commanding is more forceful, whereas long-windedness suits entreating and begging.

Hence symbols too have forcefulness, because they resemble brief sayings; for from what is briefly said one must infer the most, as from symbols. So too the "From the ground the cicadas shall sing to you" is more forceful, said allegorically, than if it were said plainly, "Your trees shall be cut down."

The periods, indeed, must be tightly drawn at the end; for the circuit is forceful, whereas the loose ending is simpler and a sign of an honest character, like the whole of the ancient style; for the ancients were simple.

So in forcefulness one must shun the archaic, both in character and in rhythm, and take refuge above all in the forcefulness now in fashion. So the layings-down of clauses such as "I agreed to support these men as far as I am able" hold closely to the rhythm I have mentioned.

A certain violence in the composition also produces forcefulness; for in many places the ill-sounding too is forceful, like uneven roads. An example is the Demosthenic "that you should have it in your power to give to you."

Antitheses and parallelisms in periods must be shunned; for they produce bulk, not forcefulness, and in many places frigidity instead of forcefulness, as Theopompus, speaking against the companions of Philip, dissolved the force by the antithesis, saying, "Murderers by nature, they were panders in their ways." For through the over-artistry — or rather bad artistry — the hearer's attention is drawn off and he falls outside all anger.

Yet often, as it were compelled by the very matters, we shall compose roundly and forcefully, as in that Demosthenic passage: "For just as, if any of those men had been convicted, you would not have written these things, so, if you are now convicted, no other will write them." For the very matter and its order had clearly a composition grown together with it, and not even by force could anyone easily have composed it otherwise. For in many matters we compose, like men running down a slope, dragged along by the very things.

It is productive of forcefulness, too, to set the most forceful thing at the end; for, enclosed in the middle, it is blunted, as in the Antisthenic, "for a man will be pained, all but, who rises from brushwood." For if one should recompose it thus, "for a man rising from brushwood will, all but, be pained," though he says the same thing, he will no longer be thought to say the same.

The antithesis I spoke of in the case of Theopompus did not suit the Demosthenic passages either, where he says, "You initiated, but I was initiated; you taught, but I attended; you played third parts, but I was a spectator; you broke down, but I hissed." For he resembles a man practicing bad artistry through the correspondence, or rather playing, not being indignant.

Density of periods suits forcefulness, though in the remaining styles it is unsuitable; for, set down continuously, it will be likened to a metre spoken in succession, and that a forceful metre, like the limping iambics.
Yet let them be at once dense and brief — I mean of two clauses; since, being of many clauses, they will furnish beauty rather than forcefulness.

Brevity is so useful to the style that even to fall silent is in many places more forceful, as Demosthenes: "But I — I do not wish to say anything harsh — this man accuses out of his abundance." Almost the man who fell silent here is more forceful than any speaker would have been.
And, by the gods, obscurity too is in many places forcefulness; for what is hinted at is more forceful, whereas what is unfolded is despised.

There is a case where cacophony produces forcefulness, and especially if the underlying matter requires it, like the Homeric "And the Trojans shuddered, when they saw the gleaming serpent." For one might have saved the metre by speaking more euphoniously, "And the Trojans shuddered, when they saw the gleaming serpent" (in altered order); but then neither would the speaker have seemed forceful, nor the serpent itself.

Following this example, then, we shall aim also at the other like effects, as, instead of "he would have written all," "all he would have written"; and instead of "he was not present," "present he was not."

Sometimes, too, we may end even in conjunctions, "de" or "te," though one is enjoined to avoid such an ending; yet in many places such a thing would be useful, as in "He did not praise him, though he deserved it, but dishonoured him"; or as in "Schoenus and Scolus." But in the Homeric passages the ending in conjunctions produced grandeur.

It might sometimes also produce forcefulness, if one should say thus, "And he overturned, out of his folly and out of his impiety, both things sacred and things holy." For in general smoothness and pleasantness of sound belong to elegance, not to forcefulness; and these styles seem most opposed.
Yet often, from playfulness mingled in, a certain forcefulness appears, as in comedies, and all the Cynic manner, as in Crates' "There is a city, Wallet, in the midst of the wine-dark vapour."

And Diogenes' saying at Olympia, when, the runner in armour having run, Diogenes himself ran on and proclaimed himself victor in the Olympic games over all men in nobility. For the saying is at once laughed at and admired, and bites gently, somehow, when spoken.

And what he said to the handsome youth: for as Diogenes wrestled with a fair boy, he was somehow stirred, and when the boy, frightened, leapt away, "Take heart, my child," he said; "I am not like that." For the surface of the saying is laughable, but the hidden suggestion is forceful. And in general, to put it briefly, the whole kind of Cynic discourse resembles something that fawns and bites at once.

The orators too will sometimes use it, and have used it: Lysias, against the man in love with the old woman, saying that "it was easier to count her teeth than her fingers"; for he showed the old woman both most forcefully and most laughably. And Homer with the "Noman I will eat last," as written above.

As for how forcefulness might arise from figures too, let us speak. From the figures of thought, then, first from what is called paraleipsis, thus: "Olynthus indeed and Methone and Apollonia and thirty-two cities on the Thracian coast I pass over." For in this he has both said everything he wished, and says that he passes them over, as having other and more forceful things to say.
And the aposiopesis mentioned before, holding to the same character, will make the discourse more forceful.

As a figure of thought, what is called prosopopoeia might be taken up for forcefulness, as "Imagine that your ancestors reproach you and say such and such things," or Greece, or the fatherland, taking the form of a woman.

As in the funeral oration Plato says, "O children, that you are of good fathers," speaking not from his own person, but from that of the fathers; for things appear much more vivid and forceful from the persons, or rather become simply dramas.

The kinds and figures of thought, then, might be taken up as has been said; for the examples mentioned are so many for the sake of illustration. As for the figures of expression, by selecting them with more variety one can make the discourse more forceful — both from the anadiplosis, as "Thebes, Thebes, a neighbouring city, has been snatched up out of the midst of Greece"; for the name spoken twice produces forcefulness.

And from what is called anaphora, as in "Against yourself you call, against the laws you call, against the democracy you call." This figure mentioned is threefold; for it is anaphora, as has been said, because the same word is referred back to the same beginning; and asyndeton, for it is spoken without conjunctions; and homoeoteleuton, through the recurring ending in "you call." And forcefulness is gathered from the three. But if one should say thus, "Against yourself and the laws and the democracy you call," together with the figures he will take away the forcefulness too.

Above all things one must know that disjunction is the worker of forcefulness, as in "He walks through the marketplace puffing out his cheeks, raising his brows, stepping in time with Pythocles." For if these be joined with conjunctions, they will be milder.

The so-called climax might also be taken up, as in Demosthenes: "I did not say these things and then not write them; nor did I write them and then not go on the embassy; nor did I go on the embassy and then not persuade the Thebans." For the discourse all but resembles a man climbing ever higher upon higher things; but if one should say these things thus, "Having spoken and written, I went on the embassy and persuaded the Thebans," he will speak a narrative only, but nothing forceful.
And in general the figures of expression furnish the speaker with acting and contention, especially the disjointed — that is, forcefulness. So much about figures of both kinds.

Let all the diction be taken up that is taken in the grand style too, except not toward the same end; for it is possible by metaphors also to make forceful effects, as in "to Python, who is bold and flows in full flood against you."
And by speaking similes, as in the Demosthenic, "This decree caused the danger that then beset the city to pass by, like a cloud."

Comparisons are not suited to forcefulness, because of their length, as in "And as a noble hound, untrained, rushes unwarily upon a boar"; for a beauty and a certain precision appears in these, whereas forcefulness wishes for something vehement and brief, and resembles men striking from close at hand.

Forcefulness arises from a compound word too, as usage too compounds many words forcefully, "the streetwalker" and "the half-struck" and any other such; and among the orators too one might find many such.

One should try to speak words fittingly to the matters, as, of the man who acted by force and villainy, "he forced his way through"; of the man who acted by force and openly and with desperation, "he cut out, he tore away"; of the man who acted craftily and secretly, "he bored through," or "slipped through," or any such word suited to the matters.
To be lifted up somehow, when taken up, produces not only grandeur but also forcefulness, as in "One must not speak with the hand inside, Aeschines, but go on an embassy with the hand inside."

And the "But that man, who appropriated Euboea." For the rising up is not for the sake of making the discourse great, but forceful. And this happens when, lifted up midway, we accuse someone; for as it were the accusation is of Aeschines, but it is Philip's.

It is forceful, too, to say some things asking the hearers, and not declaring, as in "But that man, who appropriated Euboea and built a fortress against Attica — in doing these things was he wronging us and breaking the peace, or not?" For he as it were brings the hearer into a difficulty, resembling a man being refuted and having nothing to answer. But if one should alter it and say, "He was wronging us and breaking the peace," he would resemble a man teaching plainly, not refuting.

The so-called dwelling (epimone) is expression beyond the matter, and would contribute greatly to forcefulness; an example of it is the Demosthenic, "For a disease, Athenians, a terrible one, has fallen upon Greece" — it would not have been so forceful otherwise.

Perhaps the so-called euphemism too would share in forcefulness, both the man who makes ill-omened things well-omened, and impieties pieties, as the man who urged that the golden Victories be melted down and the money spent on the war did not say it offhand, "Let us cut up the Victories for the war"; for so it would have been ill-omened and like one abusing the goddesses; but more auspiciously, "We shall make use of the Victories for the war"; for so spoken it does not resemble one cutting up the Victories, but one making them into allies.

The sayings of Demades too are forceful, although they seem to have a peculiar and strange manner; and their forcefulness arises from the suggestions, and from something allegorical taken up, and thirdly from hyperbole.

Such is "Alexander is not dead, Athenians; for the inhabited world would stink of the corpse." For the "would stink" instead of "would perceive" is at once allegorical and hyperbolic; and that the inhabited world should perceive is expressive of the power of Alexander; and at the same time the saying has something astounding, gathered from the three; and all astonishment is forceful, since it is fearful.
Of the same kind are "This decree I did not write, but the war wrote it with Alexander's spear"; and "The Macedonian power, having lost Alexander, resembles the blinded Cyclops."

And elsewhere, "a city, not the one of our ancestors that fought at sea, but an old woman, wearing sandals and slurping barley-gruel." For the "old woman" is an allegory for the weak and now spent, and at the same time shows her feebleness hyperbolically; while "slurping barley-gruel" suggests that, living at that time amid distributions of meat and full feastings, she was squandering the military funds.

About the Demadean forcefulness, then, this is enough, though it has something precarious and not very easy to imitate; for there is something poetic too in the kind, if allegory and hyperbole and suggestion are poetic — but a poetic mixed with comedy.

What is called the figured discourse the orators of today do absurdly, with an ignoble emphasis at once and, as it were, a reminding one; but the true figure of discourse is spoken with these two qualities, propriety and safety.

With propriety, as when Plato, wishing to abuse Aristippus and Cleombrotus for feasting in Aegina while Socrates lay bound at Athens for many days, and not sailing across to their comrade and teacher, though they were not a full two hundred stades distant from Athens — all this he did not say outright, for the discourse would have been abuse; but somehow with propriety in this manner. For Phaedo, asked who were present with Socrates, and having listed each, on being further asked whether Aristippus and Cleombrotus too were present, says, "No, they were in Aegina." For all the things mentioned before are suggested by the "they were in Aegina"; and the discourse seems much more forceful, the matter itself suggesting the force, not the speaker. So Plato abused the circle of Aristippus in a figure, since it was perhaps safe to abuse them.

Often, conversing with a tyrant or some other violent man, and setting out to reproach him, we need of necessity a figure of discourse, as Demetrius of Phalerum did toward Craterus the Macedonian, when he sat raised on high upon a golden couch, in a purple cloak, and received the embassies of the Greeks haughtily. Demetrius, in a figure, said reproachfully, "We too once received as ambassadors these men, and this Craterus." For in the demonstrative "this Craterus" is suggested all the haughtiness of Craterus, reproached in a figure.

Of the same kind too is Plato's saying to Dionysius, who lied and denied it: "I, Plato, agreed nothing with you; but you, by the gods—" For he is convicted of lying, and the discourse has a figure at once grand and safe.

In many places, however, they are ambiguous; to which, if one wished to liken them, blames may also be idle blames; an example is Aeschines' passage about Telauges. For nearly the whole account of Telauges would furnish a difficulty, whether it is admiration or mockery. Such a kind is ambiguous, and though not irony, has nevertheless a certain impression of irony.

One might use a figure in yet another way, thus: since rulers, men and women, hear of their own faults unpleasantly, in counselling them not to do wrong we shall not speak directly, but either we shall blame certain others who have done the like — as, toward Dionysius the tyrant, we shall speak against Phalaris the tyrant and the cruelty of Phalaris; or we shall praise certain men who have done the opposite to Dionysius, as Gelon or Hiero, that they were like fathers and teachers to Sicily. For he is at once admonished as he hears, and is not abused, and grows jealous of the praised Gelon, and reaches out himself too for praise.

There are many such things with tyrants. Philip, for instance, because he was one-eyed, grew angry if anyone in his presence named the Cyclops, or the eye at all; and Hermias, who ruled Atarneus, though in other respects mild, as it is said, would not easily have borne anyone naming a little knife, or cutting, or excision, because he was a eunuch. These things I have said, wishing above all to show the despotic character, as needing most of all safe discourse, which is called figured.

And yet often great and strong democracies too need such a kind of discourse, like the tyrants — as the people of Athens, ruler of Greece and rearing flatterers like the Cleons and Cleophons. To flatter is shameful, and to censure is precarious, but best is the middle course, that is, the figured.

And sometimes we shall praise the wrongdoer himself, not for the things in which he did wrong, but for those in which he has not done wrong: as the angry man, that yesterday he was praised for appearing mild over the faults of so-and-so, and that as one to be emulated he keeps company with the citizens. For each man gladly imitates himself, and wishes to join praise to praise, or rather to make one even praise.

And in general, just as from the same wax one man modelled a dog, another an ox, another a horse, so too with the same matter one man, declaring and accusing, says, "Men leave money to their children, but do not leave behind knowledge with it, the knowledge that will use what is left." This kind of discourse is called Aristippean. Another will set forth the same thing hypothetically, as for the most part Xenophon does, thus: "For one ought to leave one's children not money only, but also the knowledge that will use it for them."

The kind especially called Socratic, which Aeschines and Plato seem above all to have emulated, would recast this matter just mentioned into a question, somewhat thus: "Tell me, child, how much money did your father leave you? A great deal, not easily counted? A great deal, Socrates. Then did he also leave you the knowledge that will use it?" For at once it has cast the boy unawares into a difficulty, and reminded him that he is without knowledge, and exhorted him to be educated — all this in character and in tune, and not, as the saying goes, "from the Scythians."

Such discourses prospered when they were first discovered — or rather astounded, by the imitative and the vivid and the admonitory joined with high-mindedness. So much about the figuring of discourse and figured speech.

The smoothness about composition, such as those of the school of Isocrates especially use, guarding against the clash of vowel letters, is not very suitable to forceful discourse; for many things would become more forceful from the very clash, as in "For when the Phocian war broke out — not through me, for I was not yet taking part in public life then." But if one, altering and joining it, should say thus, "When the Phocian war broke out, not through me, for I was not yet taking part in public life then," he will take away no little of the forcefulness; for in many places the resonance of the clash will perhaps be more forceful.

For the unstudied and, as it were, spontaneous quality will present a certain forcefulness, especially when we show ourselves angry or wronged. But care about smoothness and harmony belongs not to an angry man, but to one at play and making a display rather.

And just as the disjointed figure produces forcefulness, as has been said before, so will a wholly disjointed composition. A sign is that of Hipponax. For wishing to abuse his enemies, he broke the metre, and made it limping instead of straight, and unrhythmical — that is, fitting for forcefulness and for abuse; for the rhythmical and pleasant-sounding would befit eulogies rather than censures. So much also about clashing.

Beside the forceful style too there lies, as is natural, a faulty one, called the graceless. It arises in the things, when one says shameful and unspeakable things openly, as the man accusing Timandra of having played the harlot heaped upon the court the basin and the obols and the rush mat and much such foul language.

The composition appears graceless if it resembles something torn apart, as the man who said, "Things being thus, this and that — to kill." And when the clauses have no connection with one another, but resemble things broken off. And periods that are continuous and long and stifle the speakers are not only cloying but also unpleasant.

By the naming, too, things that are graceful often appear more unpleasant, as Cleitarchus, speaking of the wasp, an animal resembling a bee: "It grazes, he says, the mountain country, and flies into the hollow oaks" — as though speaking of a wild ox or the Erymanthian boar, and not of some bee, so that the discourse becomes at once graceless and frigid. And both of these somehow lie close to one another.
